newsitem.title: GERMANY: German industrial competitiveness is sliding - IW.
newsitem.headline: German industrial competitiveness is sliding - IW.

text.p: Despite years of debate on the need to improve Germany's competitiveness, the world's third largest economy has slipped further in the international economic race, the Institute of the German Economy (IW) said on Thursday.
Germany is hamstrung by the industrialised world's highest labour costs, the heaviest corporate taxes and the shortest working week, the industry-funded IW said in a yearly report.
Worse still, many of the 22 measures of competitiveness tracked by the IW, like industrial productivity, have deteriorated in Germany in recent years.
"Germany as an industrialised country remains under cost pressure and there is no reason to give the all-clear," the IW report said.

Chancellor Helmut Kohl's 14-year-old coalition government is stumbling in its belated efforts to push through cuts in high tax and welfare costs, and has run into fierce trade union resistance over recent modest welfare reductions.

Parts of a 1997 austerity package have been wrecked by the opposition Social Democrats (SPD), who with their majority in the upper house of parliament may also be able to stymie a big tax reform project which Kohl wants to implement in 1999.
Manufacturing labour costs, comprising wages and social security costs, were the world's highest at 45.52 marks per hour in 1995 -- up 40 percent on 1988, the IW said.
That compares with 35.48 marks in Japan and just 25.18 marks in the United States.
Germany has been overtaken in the industry productivity league by France and Japan to slip back to fifth place overall.

Unit labour costs in western Germany have risen by 20 percent against competitors since 1989 and are only lower than those in Britain, and in eastern Germany -- where they are over 30 percent higher, the report added.
"A reduction in this burden -- as a sort of fitness cure -- is indispensable," the IW report said.

Western Germany also brings up the rear in the average number of hours worked per week at 36.4 -- compared with 40 in Japan and the United States. German workers put in the fewest hours per year on average at 1,602. Industrial plant spends the fewest hours per week in operation in Germany.
West German businesses are also the most heavily taxed, paying out 65 percent of profits. That compares with 45 percent in the U.S. and 33 percent in Britain.
All that has taken its toll on inward investment. Germany drew in just 27 billion marks between 1986 and 1995, putting it ninth in the world.
The sums invested in Germany's high-cost economy were dwarfed by the U.S. (476 billion marks), Britain (190 billion) and France (95 billion) over the same period.
"Only with more flexibility can we compensate for the world's shortest working hours and increase operating times," the IW said, saying that could help clear the "cost mountain".

But, the IW added, the state must do more to help lift the tax burden on employers, and unions should moderate their pay claims instead of forcing people onto the dole queues by demanding ever-higher wages.
